theme: Treasure in jars of clay; ambassadors for Christ
readingInstruction: Read 2 Corinthians 4:1-5:21. This is among Paul’s most moving writing. Notice the treasure in jars of clay, the contrast between the outer and inner self, the new creation, and the ministry of reconciliation.
settingTheScene: Paul has been defending his ministry against critics who find him weak. In these chapters he explains that weakness is how the power of God is shown. He is not discouraged by suffering because he sees the unseen and eternal. And he describes his message as the word of reconciliation, the center of the gospel.
observation: “For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus” sake’ (4:5).
“For God, who said, Let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (4:6).
“But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us” (4:7).
“So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day” (4:16).
“For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison” (4:17).
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come” (5:17).
“Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us” (5:20).
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (5:21).
interpretation:
Paul says that because they have received mercy, they do not lose heart. They have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways; they do not use cunning or tamper with God’s word. They commend themselves by the open statement of the truth. If the gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing, “in their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.” Preachers do not proclaim themselves but “Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus” sake.’ And the great reason for hope: “For God, who said, Let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.” Conversion is a new creation, like the first day of creation.

Then the paradox: “But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.” The treasure is the gospel; the jars of clay are cheap, fragile, ordinary containers. We are weak so that God’s power is clear. He lists the pressures: “afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed.” We always carry in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies. “So death is at work in us, but life in you.”

Because of faith in the God who raises the dead, “we do not lose heart.” The outer self wastes away; the inner self is renewed day by day. “For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison, as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.” Paul does not minimize suffering; elsewhere he lists beatings, shipwrecks, and sleeplessness. He weighs it against eternal glory.

Chapter 5 continues with the longing for the resurrection body (see the previous pause) and then turns to Christ’s love. “For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died; and he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised.” This changes how we see everyone: “From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh.” And then: “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.” All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation. “In Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation.” So we are ambassadors for Christ. “We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.” The chapter ends with the heart of the gospel: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” The great exchange: our sin was counted to Christ, and his righteousness is counted to us.
connection: Genesis 1:3 is the creation of light. Isaiah 9:2 and 60:1-3 speak of light shining in darkness. Colossians 1:15-20 describes Christ as the image of God and the reconciler. Romans 5:10-11 speaks of reconciliation. Ephesians 2:11-22 speaks of reconciliation between Jew and Gentile and with God. Isaiah 53:4-6, 10-12 and Galatians 3:13 teach substitution. Isaiah 43:19 speaks of a new thing. Revelation 21:5 says “Behold, I am making all things new.” Isaiah 49:8 is quoted in 2 Corinthians 6:2. Matthew 5:11-12 and Romans 8:18 speak of suffering and glory.
application:
Ask where you feel like a cracked jar of clay. Offer that weakness to God as a display of his power.

Practice looking at the unseen. Spend time today remembering what is eternal.

Be an ambassador: speak to someone about being reconciled to God.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for shining in your heart the light of the knowledge of his glory.
Tell him what makes you feel like a jar of clay.
Ask him to make you a faithful ambassador.
